chapters.title: Chapter 2: Behavioral Economics in Everyday Money Decisions

lessons.title: Insurance and Present Bias: Why Indians Underinsure Until It's Too Late

children.text: Suresh, a 34-year-old marketing manager in Chennai, married with a five-year-old daughter, has been telling himself the same sentence for three years: "I'll buy term insurance next month." He knows the arithmetic. He knows his employer's group cover would barely support his family for a year, let alone raise his daughter. Every month, something more immediate wins: a weekend trip, a pending work deadline, the mild dread of a medical questionnaire. Suresh is not careless, and he is not badly informed. He is present-biased, and insurance is arguably the single financial product this particular bias is worst at handling.

body.text: Present bias means people overweight costs and effort felt right now, and underweight benefits that arrive later, even when they know, rationally, that the future matters just as much. Insurance asks for a certain, immediate cost today in exchange for an uncertain, distant benefit that may never be claimed at all. That is precisely the combination a present-biased brain is worst equipped to value correctly.

markDefs.definition: The tendency to place disproportionately more weight on costs and rewards available right now than on equally or more important costs and rewards in the future, even while planning to behave more patiently later.

children.text: Economists Ted O'Donoghue and Matthew Rabin formalized

in a 1999 paper, building on earlier research into what is called hyperbolic discounting. The core finding is a strange flip: most people, offered ₹100 today or ₹110 tomorrow, take the ₹100 today. Offer the same people ₹100 in 30 days or ₹110 in 31 days, an identical one-day wait for the identical ₹10 gain, and most switch to preferring to wait for ₹110. The only thing that changed is whether "now" was one of the two options. The present, whenever it is the present, gets valued out of all proportion to everything else.

body.title: Spot the present-biased choice
body.question: Which pair of choices, made by the same person, would most clearly demonstrate present bias rather than simple impatience?
options: Preferring ₹100 today over ₹110 tomorrow, and preferring ₹100 in 60 days over ₹110 in 61 days
Preferring ₹110 tomorrow over ₹100 today, and preferring ₹110 in 61 days over ₹100 in 60 days
Preferring ₹100 today over ₹110 tomorrow, but preferring ₹110 in 61 days over ₹100 in 60 days
Preferring ₹110 tomorrow over ₹100 today, but preferring ₹100 in 60 days over ₹110 in 61 days
body.explanation: Option C is the classic present-bias reversal: impatient the moment "today" is on the table, patient about the identical one-day trade-off once both dates are in the future. Options A and B are consistent either way, simply more or less patient overall, which is ordinary time preference, not present bias specifically.

children.text: Insurance Is the Perfect Trap for a Present-Biased Brain

Buying term insurance has two costs that land entirely in the present: the premium, felt with the full, undiluted pain of paying you met in the last lesson, and the effort of comparing policies, medical tests, and paperwork, which also has to happen now. The benefit sits entirely in the future, and worse, it is conditional: for term insurance specifically, the payout only ever arrives if the policyholder dies during the term, an outcome nobody wants to picture clearly enough to plan around. A present-biased brain weighs a certain cost today far more heavily than an uncertain, unpleasant-to-imagine benefit decades from now, so the decision keeps losing to whatever else is also asking for this month's money and attention.

body.text: Industry estimates have long flagged India's life insurance protection gap, the difference between the cover people actually hold and the cover their dependents would realistically need, as one of the largest in Asia. The precise figure moves year to year, but the direction has stayed consistent for over a decade: most insured Indians are meaningfully underinsured, not uninsured.

children.text: Suresh's Gap: Doing the Maths Once

A common starting rule of thumb in Indian financial planning is term cover of roughly 10 to 15 times annual income, a simplified stand-in for a fuller needs analysis that would also weigh outstanding loans, dependents' ages, and existing assets. Suresh earns ₹12 lakh a year. His employer's group cover is ₹25 lakh. Using the simple 10x floor of the rule of thumb:

body.caption: Suresh is short by ₹95 lakh against even the conservative end of the rule of thumb, a gap his employer's group policy, tied to his job and lost the moment he switches employers, does nothing to close.

body.title: Find Meena's gap
body.prompt: Meena earns ₹18 lakh a year and holds a term policy bought eight years ago with a ₹40 lakh sum assured. Using the same 10x rule of thumb, what is her protection gap, in ₹ lakh?
body.explanation: Recommended cover = 10 × ₹18 lakh = ₹1.8 crore, or ₹180 lakh. Gap = ₹180 lakh − ₹40 lakh = ₹140 lakh. Meena did the hard part once, buying a policy, but her income has likely grown since, and the cover never followed.

children.text: The Renewal Trap: Present Bias Doesn't Stop After You Buy

Meena's situation is more common than Suresh's endless postponement, and arguably more dangerous, because it feels like the problem is already solved. Three concepts from this chapter compound on each other to keep her underinsured even after she did the responsible thing once.

body.caption: How three chapter concepts quietly lock in an outdated cover level

cells: The sum assured chosen at purchase becomes the permanent setting, never revisited without deliberate action
Auto-debited renewal premiums remove the one moment a year a person might otherwise stop and reconsider the policy
Increasing cover is itself a present-cost decision for a future benefit, so it keeps losing to whatever feels more urgent right now

children.text: Commitment Devices: Beating Your Future Self at Its Own Game

markDefs.definition: An arrangement made in advance that restricts your own future choices, so that your present self locks in a decision your future, more present-biased self might otherwise keep postponing.

children.text: In Homer's Odyssey, Odysseus has his crew tie him to his ship's mast before sailing past the Sirens, precisely because he knows his future self, hearing their song, cannot be trusted to make the safe choice. A

is the same idea applied to money: a present self, momentarily clear-headed, binding a future self who will be just as present-biased next month as this month. For insurance specifically, three commitment devices work well. Buy or increase cover right after a life event, marriage, a child, a home loan, while the need is emotionally vivid rather than abstract. Set a fixed annual review date tied to something else you never skip, like a birthday or the day Form 16 arrives, rather than a vague "someday." And where available, opt into an automatic cover step-up rider at purchase, so future increases happen by default rather than requiring a fresh present-tense decision each time, the same logic behind the automatic savings escalation you saw in Lesson 1.

body.title: Breaking Suresh's three-year loop
body.scenario: Suresh is reading this lesson on his phone, mildly annoyed at how accurately it describes him. He has decided, again, that he will "sort out insurance this weekend."
body.prompt: Based on what you've just learned about present bias and commitment devices, what should Suresh actually do differently this time, beyond simply resolving to try harder?
body.modelAnswer:
1. "This weekend" is still a present-tense promise made by his present self about a future self who has broken this exact promise for three years. Relying on willpower alone has already failed.
2. A workable commitment device removes the decision from a future moment entirely. Suresh could book a fixed appointment with an insurance advisor or an online policy purchase slot right now, in this sitting, rather than leaving "this weekend" undefined.
3. He could also use the emotional immediacy available right now, reading this lesson, feeling the mismatch clearly, as the trigger moment itself, since present bias means motivation felt today is the most reliable motivation he will ever have.
4. Finally, he should build in a forcing function for the future too, an automatic step-up rider or a calendar reminder tied to a fixed annual date, so this exact problem does not simply resurface with a higher, harder-to-close gap five years from now.

body.title: Name the fix
body.textWithBlank: An arrangement made in advance that restricts your own future choices, so a present-biased future self cannot simply postpone a decision again, is called a ___ device.
body.explanation: Commitment devices work by removing the decision from a future moment where present bias would otherwise dominate, converting a repeated "decide later" into a one-time "decide now."

body.title: Is present bias the same as procrastination?

children.text: Closely related, not identical. Procrastination is the behavior, putting something off. Present bias is one of the clearest mechanisms behind it: O'Donoghue and Rabin's 1999 paper was titled "Doing It Now or Later" precisely because it modeled how present-biased preferences produce exactly the repeated postponement Suresh describes, where every single day, "do it tomorrow" looks better than "do it today," yet tomorrow never actually arrives as the day the task gets done. Their models distinguish people who are at least aware they do this, called sophisticated present-biased agents, from those who are not, called naive ones. Awareness alone doesn't fix the bias, which is exactly why commitment devices matter even for people who know precisely what they are doing.

body.label: Suresh's protection gap
body.context: Even the conservative end of the 10 to 15 times annual income rule of thumb leaves a ₹95 lakh shortfall against his current ₹25 lakh employer group cover.

cards.definition: Overweighting costs and rewards felt right now relative to equally or more important costs and rewards in the future, formalized by O'Donoghue and Rabin in 1999.
A pattern of valuing the future where the discount rate applied between today and tomorrow is far steeper than the rate applied between two equally spaced future dates, producing present bias.
The difference between the insurance cover a person actually holds and the cover their dependents would realistically need.
An arrangement made in advance that restricts future choices, so a present-biased future self cannot simply postpone a decision again.
A sophisticated present-biased person is aware they will keep postponing and can plan commitment devices around it; a naive one is not, and typically has no such plan.

points: Present bias means costs and rewards felt right now get overweighted relative to the future, even when a person fully understands the future matters just as much.
Insurance pairs a certain, immediate cost, the premium and the effort of buying, with an uncertain, distant, uncomfortable-to-picture benefit, exactly the combination present bias handles worst.

A simple rule-of-thumb calculation, roughly 10 to 15 times annual income, often reveals a protection gap far larger than people assume, especially once income has grown since a policy was first bought.
Underinsurance persists even after buying a policy, because the default effect and payment decoupling from earlier lessons combine to keep an outdated cover level renewing on autopilot.

Commitment devices, buying at an emotionally vivid trigger moment, fixed calendar reviews, and automatic step-up riders, work by removing the decision from a future moment a present-biased self would otherwise postpone again.

body.text: This lesson explains general behavioral patterns in insurance-buying decisions and is not insurance or financial advice. Cover needs depend on individual income, liabilities, dependents, and existing assets. Consult an IRDAI-registered insurer or advisor before buying or modifying any policy.
